1. The present application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 seeks condonation of delay of 55 days in filing the present petition.
For reasons stated in the application and in the interest of justice, the delay of 55 days in filing the petition is condoned.
2. The application is allowed and disposed of accordingly.

1. The present petition under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973 (hereinafter referred to as 'CrPC') has been filed on behalf of the State, assailing the order dated 12.08.2022 passed by Mr. Mohd. Farrukh, learned Additional Sessions Judge - Special Fast Track Court, North-West, Rohini Courts, Delhi in Sessions case No. 548/2022, titled Sate v. Lalit Prajapati in case FIR No. 290/2020, dated 06.08.2020 under Section 376 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 (hereinafter referred to as 'IPC') registered at PS Kanjhawala, whereby the learned ASJ Petition) The State (Gnct Of Delhi) vs Lalit Prajapati on 19 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198307906/
1 discharged the respondent in the aforesaid FIR.
2.

sentences.text: It is the case of the prosecution that the prosecutrix, 'M', aged about 24 years, lodged a complaint at PS Kanjhawala on 06.08.2020, stating that in April 2019, the accused (respondent herein) with whom she had been in a relationship, took her to a hotel in Faridabad and on the pretext of marrying her, tried to establish physical relations with her.
She alleged that similar incidents happened on two other occasions, thereafter.
Consequently, FIR No. 290/2020, under Section 376 of the IPC was registered against the respondent.

On 11.08.2020, the statement of the prosecutrix under Section 164 CrPC was recorded wherein she stated that she had been in a relationship with the respondent for one and a half year and during that period, physical relations were established between them, with her consent.
However, due to some differences, a quarrel took place between the two and because the respondent was not answering her call, she lodged a complaint.
She further stated that now, there was no quarrel between her and the respondent and that they wished to marry each other.

3. Thereafter, in her supplementary statement, she stated that whenever physical relations were established between her and the respondent, it was always of her own free will and consent and without any force or pressure of any kind.
She stated that she accompanied the respondent to a hotel in Faridabad willingly and she knew that in the said hotel, they were going to establish physical relations.
She further stated that she did not want any legal action against the respondent.
During the course of investigation, medical examination of the prosecutrix was conducted and a site plan of the alleged place of incident was prepared at her instance.
The respondent was also interrogated and arrested.

4. Upon completion of investigation, chargesheet was filed and the case was committed to Court of Session for further proceedings.
5. The learned ASJ took note of the statement of the prosecutrix recorded under Section 164 CrPC and thereafter, her supplementary statement recorded by the Investigating Officer, wherein the prosecutrix exonerated the accused.

While discharging the respondent, the learned ASJ observed as under:
"11.
The present FIR bearing FIR No. 290/2020 U/s 376 IPC was registered on the complaint or the prosecutrix about establishing physical relation with her without her consent on the pretext of marriage.

However, during the course of investigation, her statement U/s 164 CrP.C. dated 11.08.2020 has recorded by Ld. MM and subsequently, her supplementary statement dated 24.08.2020 was recorded by IO,
wherein in both the statement, prosecutrix exonerated the accused and did not level any allegation against him attracting offence U/s 376 IPC or any other offence.
12.

The Hon'ble Delhi High Court in the case of State vs. Dr. Gajraj Singh decided on 16.01.2017, in the facts and circumstances, where the prosecutrix did not level any allegation against the accused, after placing reliance upon the Judgment of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Sajjan Kumar vs. CBI 2010 (9) SCC 368 held as under:

2 "7.

sentences.text: The present is not a case where there are some material changes or improvements or differences from the statements on the basis of which FIR was registered and recorded under Sections 161 Cr. P.C.
Statements under Section 164 Cr. P.C. were recorded by the Magistrate after verifying the voluntariness of both the prosecutrix to make the statements and that they were under no threat or coercion.
As per the statements recorded under Section 164 Cr. P.C. the police was called after the doctor scolded both the prosecutrix and their mother for not following the line.
Even during trial the two statements, that is, one recorded under Section 161 Cr. P.C. and other under Section 164 Cr. P.C. are not reconcilable.

The distinction between the two being so severe that even without a roving and fishing inquiry it can safely be held that at this stage itself there is no strong suspicion to proceed against the respondent.

As held by the Supreme Court, even at the stage of framing of charge, the Court has not to act as the mouthpiece of the prosecution but should examine the broad probabilities of case.
8.
In view of the discussion aforesaid, I find no error in the orders passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge discharging the respondent.
9. Petitions are dismissed."

13. In view of the statement of the prosecutrix U/s 164 Cr.P.C. dated 11.08.2020 which is voluntarily statement and without any threat or coercion, it can be safely concluded that accused had not committed rape upon her at any point of time.
The material improvements and differences of two statements of the prosecutrix, one in the form of complaint made before Police in her complaint dated 06.08.2020 and other statement U/s 164 CrP.C.
are making it clear that there is no strong suspicion against the accused to proceed against him.
Hence, this Court finds that there is no grave suspicion that accused Lalit Prajapati has committed any offence of rape upon the prosecutrix.
Accordingly, accused Lalit Prajapati is discharged in the present case Bail bond/surety bond stand cancelled Surety is discharged.
Documents or surety, if any be released."
6. It is well settled that the scope of exercise of powers under Section 397 CrPC is narrow.
The revisional Court is only required to satisfy itself of the correctness and legality of the findings in the impugned order.
The Court must exercise jurisdiction under Section 397 CrPC only when the decision against which the revision is directed is perverse in law and has not been passed based on the evidence on record.
7. This court does not find any perversity in the impugned order.
The learned ASJ, based on the material on record, has rightly discharged the respondent herein.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Dilawar Balu Khurane v. State of Maharashtra, (2002) 2 SCC 135 has observed that while framing charges, the Judge has the power to ascertain whether the materials on record disclose 'grave suspicion' against the accused, which has not been explained.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It has been held as under:
"12.
Now the next question is whether a prima facie case has been made out against the appellant.

In exercising powers under Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Petition) The State (Gnct Of Delhi) vs Lalit Prajapati on 19 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/198307906/
3 Procedure, the settled position of law is that the Judge while considering the question of framing the charges under the said section has the undoubted power to sift and weigh the evidence for the limited purpose of finding out whether or not a prima facie case against the accused has been made out; where the materials placed before the court disclose grave suspicion against the accused which has not been properly explained the court will be fully justified in framing a charge and proceeding with the trial; by and large if two views are equally possible and the Judge is satisfied that the evidence produced before him while giving rise to some suspicion but not grave suspicion against the accused, he will be fully justified to discharge the accused, and in exercising jurisdiction under Section 227 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Judge cannot act merely as a post office or a mouthpiece of the prosecution, but has to consider the broad probabilities of the case, the total effect of the evidence and the documents produced before the court but should not make a roving enquiry into the pros and cons of the matter and weigh the evidence as if he was conducting a trial (see Union of India v. Prafulla Kumar Samal [(1979) 3 SCC 4 :
1979 SCC (Cri) 609] )."
